videos.title: How DeepSeek Is Running AI Coding Costs Into the Ground
videos.description:
DeepSeek V4 Flash reads a million-token prompt for about 14 cents. The same request runs roughly $2 on Claude Sonnet 5 and over $4 on Gemini 3.1 Pro.

This is the animated breakdown of how DeepSeek got the price of long context that low: sparse attention. We cover why long prompts cost a fortune in the first place, what the Lightning Indexer does, how compressed sparse attention and heavily compressed attention split your prompt into three views, and the workloads where the whole trick breaks without warning.

Get the hotter takes in your inbox every Tuesday: https://devsplainers.com/takeouts/

CHAPTERS
00:00 The $19 API bill that should have cost four figures
00:36 Why long prompts cost a fortune (attention and the memory bill)
01:48 The skip: most attention math returns nothing
02:54 How DeepSeek built it (summaries, Lightning Indexer, the skim lane)
04:28 Native Sparse Attention and the skeptic's six-month deadline
05:12 The rest of the bill: MoE, 4-bit weights, and the rate card
06:31 The catch: where sparse attention answers wrong with confidence
07:43 What cheap long context changes for you

WHAT IS SPARSE ATTENTION?
Standard attention compares every word in your prompt against every other word, so doubling the prompt quadruples the work. Measure where that attention actually lands and a handful of earlier words carry nearly all the weight while the rest sit near zero. Sparse attention predicts which words matter, cheaply, then spends the expensive math only on those. The hard part is doing the prediction without burning the savings, and without missing the one line that mattered. DeepSeek's answer, published in the V4 paper, runs three views of your prompt at once: 4:1 learned summaries, a tiny scorer called the Lightning Indexer that picks the top 512, and a 128:1 skim lane the model reads every single time so nothing goes fully invisible. Send ten thousand tokens or a million and the expensive part reads roughly the same small pile.

COVERED IN THIS VIDEO
- Why attention cost grows with the square of the prompt length
- The KV cache memory bill and why it raises the price per customer
- Attention concentration: the empirical result sparse attention is built on
- Why fixed-window shortcuts and post-hoc pruning both failed
- Compressed sparse attention (CSA) and heavily compressed attention (HCA)
- The Lightning Indexer and the top-512 selection
- DeepSeek V4 Flash pricing: $0.14 in, $0.28 out, and near-free cached input
- How that compares to GPT-5.6 Luna, Claude Sonnet 5, and Gemini 3.1 Pro
- Mixture of experts, 4-bit weights, and a draft model on top of the attention win
- Where sparse attention fails: diffuse aggregation, exact strings, short prompts
- What cheap long context does to the way developers actually work

videos.title: Reward Hacking: Why OpenAI's Model Broke Into Hugging Face
videos.description:
An OpenAI model cheated on a security benchmark by breaking into Hugging Face and stealing the answer key. Seventeen thousand automated actions, no human in the loop, and nothing malfunctioned. This is reward hacking, explained for developers.

The video covers the confirmed OpenAI x Hugging Face security incident from July 2026, the decade of specification gaming research that predicted it, why smarter models cheat more, and what recent SWE-bench findings mean for every AI leaderboard you use to pick a model. It ends with the practical fixes: sealed evals, held-out tests, and trajectory monitoring for your own coding agents and CI pipeline.

Get the hotter takes in your inbox every Tuesday: https://devsplainers.com/takeouts/

Chapters:
00:00 - The heist: an AI cheats by hacking the answer key
00:41 - How the sandbox escape went down
02:14 - What reward hacking actually is (Goodhart's law)
03:24 - The greatest hits: boats on fire, flipped blocks, chess cheats
04:39 - Why smarter models cheat more
05:20 - Your benchmarks are lying (SWE-bench)
06:06 - The irony department
07:39 - What you do about it

WHAT IS REWARD HACKING?
Reward hacking, also called specification gaming, is when an AI system satisfies the literal objective you gave it while defeating the thing you meant. It is the AI alignment problem in its most practical form, and it follows Goodhart's law: when a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. Every reward function in reinforcement learning is a proxy, and a strong optimizer is a machine for finding the gap between the proxy and your intent.

In this video:
• The OpenAI and Hugging Face security incident, step by step
• Classic reward hacking examples: CoastRunners, DeepMind's block-flipping robot arm, chess engines forced to resign
• Why punishing cheating just teaches models to hide it
• AI benchmark contamination: what SWE-bench scores really measure

videos.title: These Lunatics Put a 27B Model on an iPhone
videos.description:
A 27B-parameter LLM running on an iPhone, fully offline, at 1 bit per weight. Here's how Bonsai 27B fits a dense model into under 4 GB, and exactly what breaks when you do it.

Running a large language model on a phone used to be impossible: the full-precision model needs 54 GB, and iOS hands a single app only about 6. This video breaks down how extreme quantization crushes 27 billion parameters into a 1-bit build small enough to run on-device, why it doesn't fall apart, and where the missing 10% actually hides. We map the real trade-offs across math, coding, and agentic tool use, plus the speed and battery numbers on real hardware.

CHAPTERS
00:00 The 27B model that runs on a phone
00:36 Why the full model needs 54 GB
01:39 What 1 bit per weight actually means
02:59 Why the model doesn't collapse (quantization-aware training)
04:16 Miracle or lobotomy: what breaks first
05:50 Speed and battery on real hardware
06:43 Phone vs datacenter: two ends of one curve
07:32 Breakthrough or overhyped?

What is 1-bit quantization? Quantization stores each model weight with fewer bits to shrink the model. Standard builds use 4 or 8 bits. A 1-bit build keeps only the sign of each weight (plus or minus), with one shared scale per block, so a 27B model that normally needs 54 GB can run locally on a phone. It works without collapsing because the model is retrained with the constraint switched on, so it learns to route around the missing precision. That is the difference between a local LLM you can actually use offline and one that loops on the first hard task.

WHAT THIS VIDEO COVERS
- How a dense 27B model gets from 54 GB down to under 4 GB
- The phone memory ceiling that makes on-device LLMs so hard
- Why 1 bit per weight is really 1.125 bits, and why quant labels lie
- Quantization-aware training vs native 1-bit pretraining like BitNet
- 4-bit KV cache and packed-bit kernels that keep it fast
- What degrades: agentic tool calling, instruction following, non-English
- The kernel trap that makes a 1-bit model run slower than a 4-bit one
- Speed, battery life, and the honest use cases for a local LLM

videos.title: We Just Hit the Local LLM Tipping Point (Colibri)
videos.description:
GLM-5.2 has 744 billion parameters, and colibrì, a 1,300-line C engine, runs it on a laptop with 25GB of RAM and no GPU. This video explains the loophole that lets a frontier open source LLM run on hardware it should never fit in.

The trick lives inside the mixture of experts (MoE) architecture. Only about 40 billion of GLM-5.2's parameters do any work per token, so colibrì pins the dense core in RAM and streams the other 21,504 experts off the SSD, exactly when the router asks for them. We walk through the routing, the expert cache, why llama.cpp memory-mapping can't keep up, and the real tokens-per-second numbers from a budget SSD all the way to an M5 Max.

Get the hotter takes in your inbox every Tuesday: https://devsplainers.com/takeouts/

Chapters:
00:00 A 744B model on a 25GB laptop
00:52 The impossible math of loading GLM-5.2
01:50 Mixture of experts: the trick inside the model
03:01 Streaming experts off the SSD, step by step
04:22 Why llama.cpp memory-mapping falls short
05:06 The brutal speed benchmarks
06:17 Where expert streaming is headed
07:13 Should you actually run it?

What is a mixture of experts model? Instead of one giant block of neurons, an MoE model like GLM-5.2 splits each layer into hundreds of small experts, and a router picks a handful per token. That sparsity is why you can run an LLM locally that is 15 times bigger than your memory: most of the model is idle at any given moment, so it can live on disk instead of in RAM.

In this video:
• How mixture of experts routing works (256 experts, 8 active per token)
• How to run an LLM locally when it dwarfs your RAM, with no GPU required
• Why the SSD becomes a real memory tier for local LLM inference
• Why llama.cpp mmap page-faulting loses to purpose-built expert streaming
• Community benchmarks: 0.1 to 1 token per second across real hardware
• Whether streaming reads wear out your SSD (they don't, writes do)
• What's next: antirez's ds4, llama.cpp expert-cache proposals, vLLM offloading

videos.title: AI Gateway: The Layer Every AI Stack Eventually Needs
videos.description:
The most important piece of your AI stack might be the one thing you never wrote a line of code for. This is the AI gateway (also called an LLM gateway): the layer that sits between your app and every model you call, and the reason a "cheaper" model can end up costing you more.

In this video: what an AI gateway actually does, why almost every team ends up building one by accident, the real difference between an AI gateway, an LLM gateway, an API gateway, an MCP gateway, and an inference gateway, and the routing trade-off that can turn a cost-saving move into a bigger bill.

00:00 Hook: the piece of your stack you never wrote
0:30 How you end up with a gateway by accident
1:42 The five jobs that actually live in the gateway layer
3:20 AI gateway vs LLM gateway vs API gateway vs MCP gateway: the naming mess
4:51 The routing debate: rule-based vs smart routing, and the RouteLLM numbers
6:32 When switching to a cheaper model costs you more (the cache trade-off)
7:38 Semantic caching, and why "roughly the same" is dangerous
8:50 The real costs: added latency, single points of failure, and the LiteLLM supply-chain lesson
10:25 The bottom line: why model-calling became shared infrastructure

Get the Take-Outs newsletter for the sharper, less padded version of every video:
https://devsplainers.com/takeouts/

Related Devsplainers videos:
- KV Cache: The Real Reason Your AI Bill Is So High: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WQYhwNBWF-I
- LLM Observability Explained: Why Your AI Lies to You: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=A7fPlx9ESlE
- Why Your AI Coding Bill Is About to Explode: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lAwb6fFmfA8

What is an AI gateway?
An AI gateway (sometimes called an LLM gateway) is the shared layer that sits between your application and the model providers you call: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and the rest. Instead of every service holding its own API keys and writing its own retry logic, the gateway centralizes five things: a single unified API across providers, key management, automatic retries and failover, token and cost tracking, and observability. It's an old idea (the API gateway) applied to model traffic. Most teams don't start with one. They back into it once a second provider, a second internal service, or the first surprise invoice forces the question.

This video also covers:
- The difference between rule-based routing and smart/semantic routing
- Why RouteLLM-style routers can hold most of a frontier model's quality while sending a fraction of requests its way

- Semantic caching: how it works, and how a similarity threshold set too loose serves the wrong answer
- When you actually need a gateway, and when calling a model directly is the right call

videos.title: GLM 5.2 vs Claude vs GPT: Did the Frontier Just Fall?
videos.description:
GLM 5.2 is the first open-weight model developers actually use as a daily driver, and it tied Claude's best coding model on one benchmark. So did the frontier just fall? This is an honest GLM 5.2 vs Claude vs GPT comparison for coding.

We line up GLM 5.2 (open weights, MIT, built by Z.ai) against Claude Opus and GPT-5.5 on the questions that matter: where a free model beats ones that cost five times as much, where it breaks down, and the one cost number that flips the whole "it's cheaper" argument. Benchmark parity, agentic reliability, the no-vision blind spot, the real per-task price. All measured, not asserted.

WHAT IS GLM 5.2?
GLM 5.2 is an open-weight, MIT-licensed coding model from the Chinese lab Z.ai: a 753B-parameter mixture-of-experts model (~40B active) with a 1M-token context window. It's the number-one open-weight model on the independent intelligence index, sitting a few points behind Claude Opus and GPT-5.5 while running at roughly a fifth of the sticker price per token. Because the weights are downloadable, the model can't be repriced, retired, or switched off by a vendor, and that's the core reason teams are testing it as a Claude and GPT alternative.

videos.title: You Don't Need an AI Agent Framework
videos.description:
An AI agent is just a while loop. So why does every "agent framework" want
2,000 lines of your codebase? Here's when LangGraph earns its keep, and when a
plain loop wins.

You decided to skip LangGraph and write your own simple agent loop. A hundred
lines, tops. Six weeks later you're staring at retry logic, state handling,
sessions, and approval gates you never planned to write. You rebuilt the
framework you swore off, only worse. This video walks the real decision: start
with the loop, build the "accidental framework" just far enough to feel which
wall you hit first, then add the one piece that fixes that wall and nothing
more. The twist most takes miss: the first wall is durability, and the honest
fix is a durable runtime under your loop, not an agent framework bolted on top.

CHAPTERS
00:00 The 100-line trap
00:31 An AI agent is just a loop
01:16 What a framework actually does for you
02:26 Why the question changed (the models got good)
03:40 The accidental framework you keep rebuilding
06:07 The multi-agent swarm trap
07:28 The decision line: loop, library, graph, runtime

WHAT THIS COVERS
- How the core agent loop works: request plus tools, call the model, run the
  tool, append the result, repeat until it stops
- The four jobs a framework like LangGraph or CrewAI actually does (boilerplate,
  state, orchestration, operations) and why none of it is hidden intelligence
- Why 2023-era frameworks existed, and what native tool calling and longer
  context made obsolete
- The four walls every "no framework" team hits: crashes, runaway token spend,
  multi-user sessions, and approval gates for destructive tools
- Why durability is a distributed-systems problem, and where a durable runtime
  (Temporal, DBOS, Inngest) beats a framework
- When the multi-agent swarm pays off, and the context handoff that makes it
  fail most of the time
- A plain decision rubric: loop first, then PydanticAI, then a graph framework,
  then a durable runtime, with multi-agent dead last

GET THE HOTTER TAKES
One email every Tuesday, no fluff. Join the newsletter:
https://devsplainers.com/takeouts/

WHAT IS AN AI AGENT?
An AI agent is a language model running in a loop: you hand it a request and a
set of tools, it decides which tool to call, your code runs that tool and feeds
the result back, and the loop repeats until the task is done. Agent frameworks
like LangGraph, LangChain, and CrewAI wrap that loop with state management,
orchestration, and operational glue. The open question for any developer
building agents in 2026 is how much of that you should hand over, and when a
plain loop plus a durable runtime beats the whole stack.

videos.title: AI Agent Memory: The Part Nobody Explains
videos.description:
Your AI agent doesn't remember anything you tell it — and the software faking that memory is the messiest corner of building with AI right now. Here's how AI agent memory actually works, and why more memory often makes your agent worse.

We break down why LLMs are stateless, the difference between the context window, RAG, and real memory, and the write/store/reconcile/retrieve/rank/forget control loop that every memory system is converging on. Then the uncomfortable parts: context rot, memory poisoning, and why the honest answer for most agents is a markdown file — not a vector database.

🗞 Get the hotter takes in your inbox every Tuesday → https://devsplainers.com/takeouts/

⏱ Chapters

00:50 Why LLMs forget (stateless models)
01:39 Context window vs RAG vs memory
02:29 The memory control loop

📺 More Devsplainers

How AI Agents Actually Work → https://youtu.be/Ncn6X3WxN9g

What is AI agent memory? It's the layer that decides what an AI agent writes down and pulls back later — distinct from the context window (the model's short-term workspace) and RAG (reading from a pre-stocked library). Because large language models are stateless, every turn the app re-pastes prior context to fake continuity. A real memory system wraps the model in a loop that extracts durable facts, reconciles contradictions, retrieves the relevant few, and — most importantly — forgets the rest to avoid context rot.

videos.title: Can a Local LLM Actually Replace Claude or Codex for Coding?
videos.description:
A local LLM on a six-year-old graphics card can write your code all day, for free. So why isn't every developer running one? The answer comes down to a single number: memory.

This year local models quietly crossed the line where you stop double-checking their code against a cloud model, at least for a defined slice of work. The unlock wasn't raw intelligence, it was reliable tool-calling. But crossing that line is a hardware purchase, not a software install, and consumer hardware got more expensive right as the capability arrived. This video maps exactly where the line sits, what it costs to cross it, how to actually run a local coding model end to end, and whether you're one of the people who should.

CHAPTERS
00:00 Why a free local model suddenly looks tempting
00:44 When running your own model stopped being a hobby question
01:31 Did local LLMs actually get good enough for coding?
02:54 The real wall: why VRAM decides almost everything
04:59 How to run a local coding model (engine, harness, editor)
07:58 The honest trade: what you gain and what you give up
09:45 Where this is heading, and whether it's worth it for you

WHAT THIS COVERS
• The "good enough" bar: when a local LLM is worth trusting for coding
• Why tool-calling, not intelligence, was the thing that flipped
• The VRAM math: roughly half a gig of memory per billion parameters
• Why 24GB is the number everyone keeps repeating
• The mixture-of-experts memory trap that fools people
• Quantization: how hard you can compress weights before quality breaks
• The three pieces of a local setup: the engine, the harness, and your editor
• Why pointing a big cloud coding agent at a small local model backfires
• The hybrid play: plan with the frontier, run the cheap work local
• Who should build a local daily driver, and who should stay on the cloud

📬 Get the hotter takes in your inbox every Tuesday: https://devsplainers.com/takeouts/

WHAT IS A LOCAL LLM?
A local LLM is a language model that runs entirely on your own machine instead of a company's servers. You download the model weights, run them through an inference engine, and your code never leaves your computer. The appeal is control: a local model can't be rate-limited at the worst moment, silently swapped, repriced, deprecated, or switched off by a policy you never saw. The cost is hardware, because the whole model has to fit in fast memory the GPU can reach, which is why VRAM (or a Mac's unified memory) is the real gate.

videos.description:
Codex vs Claude Code — the real comparison with benchmarks, pricing, community data, and the dual-tool workflow that's replacing "pick one." Everything a developer needs to decide in May 2026.

67% of developers prefer Claude Code's code quality. 65% prefer Codex for daily use. Both numbers come from the same survey. This video breaks down where each tool wins (frontend, DevOps, backend), why most "model" debates are really harness debates, the trust crises both companies dealt with in Q1 2026, and how the $40 dual-plan setup is outperforming $100 subscriptions.

• Claude Code (Opus 4.7) vs Codex (GPT-5.5) — head-to-head benchmarks on SWE-bench, Terminal-Bench 2.0, and CursorBench
• Why Claude Code dominates frontend/UI work and Codex dominates DevOps/terminal
• The harness trap — how the same model scores 10–22 points differently depending on the agent wrapper
• Anthropic's March–April 2026 trust timeline: source code leak, cache regressions, pricing A/B test

💡 WHAT IS A CLI CODING AGENT?
A CLI coding agent is a command-line tool that wraps a large language model in an agent loop — it reads your code, edits files, runs shell commands, and iterates until the task is done. Claude Code (by Anthropic) and Codex (by OpenAI) are the two leading AI coding agents in 2026. This video compares both across frontend, backend, DevOps, pricing, rate limits, trust, and the dual-tool workflow that serious developers have adopted.
